items.title: Talent search
items.goal: A recruiter types what they are looking for in plain language and gets ranked candidates from the agency's own database in under three seconds, with filters for skills, years, location, language and CV date, and a clear view of how fresh each CV is. Searching from a job ranks by that job's match score with the same reasons.
prd: Talent search → all five requirements → proposed
Talent search → search covers only the agency's own database; no external sources at launch → decided
Talent search → external sources later: the design should let approved sources be added later, each with an on/off switch → decided
Technical architecture → Search: pgvector for meaning, PGroonga for English and Chinese keywords → proposed
AI pipeline → Search: a model turns plain language into filters plus search text; Postgres runs keyword, vector and filter search together → suggested
Non-functional requirements → Speed: search results in under 3 seconds → decided
exit: A plain-language query returns sensible ranked candidates in under three seconds on the seeded set
All five PRD filters work, including a Simplified Chinese keyword hit
Searching from a job ranks by that job's match score and shows the same reasons
Protected terms in a query do not become scoring or filter criteria
outOfScope: External talent sources such as LinkedIn, job boards or partner agencies — a non-goal, though the design must not preclude adding an approved source later with an on/off switch
Hiding candidates without consent or past retention — that is the real-data release
Saved searches, alerts or any notification — the portal sends no email

items.title: Recruiters search in plain language
items.story: As a recruiter, I want to type "accountant with SAP experience and 5+ years in Singapore" and get the right people, so that I do not have to translate my own thinking into a filter form.
ac: Given a plain-language query, when I search, then it is turned into filters plus search text and the results reflect both.
Given a query mentioning a protected attribute, when it is processed, then that term does not become a filter or a scoring criterion.
Given any query, when I search the seeded set, then results appear in under three seconds.
Given a query in Simplified Chinese, when I search, then Chinese keyword matches are found.
prd: Talent search → requirement 1: plain-language search → proposed
Technical architecture → Search: pgvector plus PGroonga → proposed
AI pipeline → Search: one model call turns the query into filters plus search text; Postgres runs keyword, vector and filter together → suggested
Non-functional requirements → Speed: under 3 seconds → decided

items.title: Write the search query prompt and filter schema
items.what: Write the schema and prompt that turn a recruiter's sentence into structured filters plus the text to search for, in English and Simplified Chinese, refusing to turn a protected attribute into a filter.
scope: `src/ai/prompts/search-query/`: schema covering skills, years, location, language and CV date, plus free search text
Prompt v1 with fictional English and Simplified Chinese examples
A rule that protected attributes mentioned in a query are reported back to the recruiter rather than applied as filters
Ambiguity handling: what the model does when the query is vague, so the recruiter can refine rather than get nothing
A prompt version recorded on every run
done: The schema covers all five PRD filters plus free search text
A query naming a protected attribute produces no filter for it and an explicit note back to the recruiter, covered by an example
Fictional English and Simplified Chinese examples are included
The prompt carries a version the service records

items.title: Build the hybrid search SQL combining PGroonga, pgvector and filters
items.what: Write one database function that applies the hard filters, the PGroonga keyword match and the pgvector similarity together and returns a fused ranking, fast enough to answer in well under three seconds on the seeded set. Test-first.
scope: Enable PGroonga and add the indexes both search paths need
One SQL function taking filters, keyword text, an embedding, an optional job version, a limit and an offset
A documented fusion rule combining keyword and vector rank
Failing tests first: each filter excludes correctly; a Simplified Chinese keyword matches; the fusion order is deterministic; the job-version argument switches ranking to match score
A timing assertion over the seeded set against the three-second budget
done: Failing-then-passing tests cover every filter, a Chinese keyword hit, deterministic fusion and job-scoped ranking
Search over the seeded set completes within the documented budget, asserted by a test
Keyword, vector and filter work happens in one query rather than in application code

items.title: Recruiters filter results and see how fresh each CV is
items.story: As a recruiter, I want to narrow results and see when each CV was last updated, so that I do not call someone about a role they left three years ago.
ac: Given the search screen, when I use the filters, then skills, years of experience, location, language and CV date all narrow the results.
Given a result, when I look at it, then it shows when that CV was last updated.
Given the search screen at 390 px, when I use it, then the filters are reachable and the page does not scroll horizontally.
prd: Talent search → requirement 2: filters for skills, years, location, language and CV date → proposed
Talent search → requirement 4: results show when each CV was last updated → proposed
UI design → Candidate search screen → decided

items.title: Build the search screen with filters and CV freshness
items.what: Build the search screen from `design/specs/search.md`: the plain-language box, the five filters, and results showing each candidate with their CV's last-updated date.
scope: A route and page running the query through the search service
All five filters, in a sheet at phone width
Each result showing the CV's last-updated date as a relative age with the exact date available
Loading, empty and error states from the shared patterns, including the case where the model could not understand the query
Playwright coverage at both widths with the shared assertions
done: All five filters narrow results, covered by an end-to-end test
Every result shows its CV's last-updated date
A query the model cannot interpret produces a helpful message rather than an empty list with no explanation
Playwright passes at desktop and phone width

items.title: Searching from a job ranks by that job's match score
items.story: As a recruiter working one job, I want search results ordered by how well people fit that job, so that search and the ranked list tell me the same story.
ac: Given I search from a job, when results return, then they are ranked by that job's match score.
Given a result in a job-scoped search, when I look at it, then it shows the same reasons and evidence as the job's ranked list.
Given a candidate with no score for that job version, when they appear, then they are shown as not yet scored rather than as a zero.
prd: Talent search → requirement 3: searching from a job ranks results by that job's match score, with the same reasons as Job matching → proposed
Job matching → requirement 4: scores are keyed to the job version → proposed

items.title: Add job-scoped search that reuses match scores and reasons
items.what: Let a recruiter search within a job's context so results are ranked by that job's stored match scores and show the same reasons, without triggering any new AI call.
scope: An entry point from job detail into search, carrying the job version
Ranking by stored match score for that job version, with filters still applied
Reasons and evidence rendered from the stored score, using the same components as the ranked list
Failing tests first: ranking follows the score; a candidate with no score for that version shows as not yet scored; no AI scoring call is made during a job-scoped search
exclusions: Adding candidates to the pipeline from search, unless the design spec includes it
done: Failing-then-passing tests cover score-ordered ranking, the unscored candidate and the no-AI-call rule
Reasons shown in job-scoped search come from the stored score and match the job's ranked list
Playwright covers entering search from a job and seeing score-ordered results
